status_summary: Secretary Rubio announced a reorganization on 2025-04-22 that, per AP, would cut domestic staff by 15 percent and consolidate 734 bureaus and offices into 602 (State's own statement is general and does not mention political leadership of bureaus), and on 2025-07-11 State sent reduction-in-force notices to about 1,100 civil servants and nearly 250 Foreign Service officers, saying changes would be complete by 2025-08-04, that nearly 3,000 members of the workforce would depart in all and that no further reductions in force were planned (per Nextgov). Civil-service employees were separated on 2025-09-11 according to a complaint filed by affected employees on 2026-02-13 (an allegation, not a finding), while the Foreign Service separations were delayed by Section 120 of Public Law 119-37, which barred reduction-in-force actions through 2026-01-30, and by a 2025-12-17 preliminary injunction from a federal court in San Francisco through the same date; on 2026-01-09 the judge said the order did not reach the July notices, the government withdrew its appeal, and State declined to rescind the July notices. AFSA stated on 2026-05-05 that State separated more than 200 Foreign Service members under the reduction in force that week, and State's FY2027 budget justification projects about 11,000 Foreign Service and 6,000 civil service employees, down from over 14,000 and nearly 13,000 before 2025 (as reported by Federal News Network). In 2026-06-03 testimony, State's Office of Inspector General called the reorganization and integration of selected USAID functions the department's main staffing and organizational challenge.

timeline.event: Rubio announced a department-wide reorganization: 15% cut in US-based staff, more than 100 bureaus closed or consolidated (734 bureaus and offices reduced to 602), and a new office for foreign and humanitarian affairs; State's spokesperson called it a roadmap rather than immediate firings.

State publishes a statement titled Building an America First State Department announcing a comprehensive reorganization plan in general terms: consolidating region-specific functions, removing redundant offices and ending programs not required by statute that it views as out of line with core national interests. The page names no bureaus, staffing numbers or leadership changes (it is undated; date from contemporaneous reporting).

The Supreme Court stayed a district-court injunction against Executive Order 14210 (agency workforce reductions and reorganization plans) while appeals proceed, saying the government was likely to succeed on its argument that the order is lawful and expressing no view on any specific agency plan.
timeline.source: Supreme Court of the United States

timeline.event: State issued reduction-in-force notices to more than 1,300 employees: over 1,100 civil servants (60 days' notice) and nearly 250 Foreign Service staff serving domestically (120 days' notice).

State civil-service employees who received reduction-in-force notices on 2025-07-11 were separated on this date, according to a complaint filed by former federal employees in the District of Maryland on 2026-02-13 (allegations in a court filing, not findings); the same complaint alleges that one Foreign Service officer was separated through an involuntary resignation on 2025-11-16.
timeline.source: Complaint, No. 8:26-cv-00573 (D. Md.), copy hosted by dclawcollective.com

timeline.event: The stopgap funding law that ended the 43-day shutdown, Public Law 119-37, takes effect. Its Section 120 bars federal funds for initiating, noticing or carrying out a reduction in force through 2026-01-30 and gives no force or effect to RIFs taken between 2025-10-01 and enactment, with exceptions for voluntary separations, court-ordered actions and orderly shutdown actions; State and unions disagreed on whether it covered the notices issued in July (per Federal News Network).
State sent an updated notice setting Foreign Service separations for 2025-12-05; later in December a federal judge in San Francisco (Judge Illston) enjoined State and other agencies' layoffs.

Per a case tracker summary, the court in AFGE v. OMB (N.D. Cal. No. 3:25-cv-08302, Judge Illston) granted a temporary restraining order against a State Department reduction in force scheduled for 2025-12-05; the order itself was not read.

Judge Illston (N.D. Cal.), in a suit led by federal employee unions including AFSA, issues a preliminary injunction directing State, Education, the SBA and GSA to rescind reduction-in-force notices for employees terminated during the shutdown and barring further steps to carry out a reduction in force through 2026-01-30; nearly 250 State Foreign Service officers were affected, per news reports.

At a 2026-01-09 hearing Judge Illston said her order covered only State's updated 2025-12-02 notice and did not require rescinding the July notices, without issuing a new formal order; the government had appealed the December order and then withdrawn the appeal, and State said it would not send rescission notices for about 250 Foreign Service officers.

Federal News Network reported (month-level date) that State's FY2027 budget justification projects about 11,000 Foreign Service and 6,000 civil service employees, that the officers with RIF notices had been on paid leave for nine months, and that a senior official told House members there were no plans to reinstate them.
AFSA states that State separated more than 200 Foreign Service members under the reduction in force first announced in July 2025; AFSA opposes the separations.

State's Office of Inspector General testifies to a Senate appropriations subcommittee that the reorganization and the integration of selected USAID functions, on a compressed timeline, were the main staffing challenge, and recommends an implementation plan with milestones; the testimony does not discuss staff cuts or bureau consolidation.
timeline.source: State Department Office of Inspector General

title: Reorganize State to cut offices and overhead and tighten political control
uncertainties: State's reorganization statement on its own site (state.gov) could not be fetched in the latest check either (client error), and neither could a State press statement of May 2025 reportedly announcing the congressional notification of the plan. The statement is general and gives no numbers by the account of the earlier review, so the figures come from AP and Federal News Network and describe the plan, not a verified end state. An external retrieval reported figures from a congressional notification letter of 2025-05-29 (more than 300 of 734 bureaus and offices streamlined, merged or eliminated, 3,448 domestic positions cut from 18,780, an 18 percent staff reduction) and a foreign service separation date of 2025-11-10; these are known only through that retrieval, the letter itself is not public in full according to the retrieval, and they are not stated as verified. They differ in form from the AP figures in the record (15 percent cut, 734 offices reduced to 602) and the difference was not reconciled. Read in the latest check: Nextgov (2025-07-11) confirms notices to about 1,100 civil servants and nearly 250 Foreign Service officers on 2025-07-11, 60 and 120 day notice periods, a completion date of 2025-08-04 and no plans for further reductions in force; a complaint filed on 2026-02-13 in the District of Maryland (No. 8:26-cv-00573, read on a copy hosted by a plaintiffs' counsel collective; the court docket was not reached) alleges that State plaintiffs received notices on 2025-07-11 and civil service plaintiffs were separated on 2025-09-11, with one Foreign Service officer separated by involuntary resignation on 2025-11-16 (plaintiffs' allegations; the 2025-11-10 date from the retrieval was not found there). The FY2027 budget justification and State's organizational chart were not opened. The temporary restraining order date, case number and appeal number rest on a case tracker (Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse) whose docket summary has no 2026 entries; the court orders were not read, and CourtListener could not be reached from this review. The injunction's 2026-01-30 end date and the appeal withdrawal are confirmed by news reports. The 2026-05-05 separations rest on a statement by AFSA, an interested party. No source in this record shows a change to political control of bureaus, which the Mandate's recommendation mentions. A limited search found no court ruling on the May 2026 separations, no fiscal 2027 reduction-in-force bar and no State authorization bill.
